video_title: Bill Ackman: “Some Dominant Companies Will Just Disappear”
gist: Bill Ackman explains how AI has raised disruption risk enough that some dominant companies may disappear, describes Pershing Square's process, Netflix round trip and Howard Hughes-to-insurance 'modern Berkshire' plan, warns of a venture-funding reset, and discusses his daughter's brain injury and the brain institute he is building.

themes.theme: AI disruption risk and bubble dynamics

insights.claim: Ackman says AI has massively increased the risk of disruption, making it the hardest question in investing, and expects every investor to look foolish on at least one business whose disruption they failed to anticipate.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Moat assessment is now the central risk; even 'dominant' franchises can be impaired, so position sizing and durability screens matter.
insights.quote: All of us are guaranteed to look foolish with one business or another that we didn't anticipate the risk of disruption because of AI.

insights.claim: Some currently dominant companies will simply disappear because of AI, and Ackman says he is not frightened but must be very thoughtful about how wide moats really are.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Supports avoiding long-duration bets on businesses whose value depends on information or software layers AI can replicate.
insights.quote: There will be some that will just disappear.

insights.claim: Ackman uses Buffett as a cautionary example: the greatest investor did not perceive the internet's disruption risk (e.g. Wikipedia displacing World Book), so AI is a more complicated version of the same problem.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Even experienced value investors misjudge technology disruption of moats.

insights.claim: He sees bubble-like elements in venture: a startup that was not raising was preempted with $50 million at a $400 million valuation and two weeks later raised another $50 million at a $1 billion valuation, and he saw a Series A at a $5 billion pre-money valuation.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of late-cycle FOMO pricing in private AI rounds.

insights.claim: A high-profile blow-up where people lose a lot of money will eventually cause a reset in AI/venture, comparable to the internet bubble when Barron's listed public internet companies' months of cash left just before the crash; disciplined companies with years of runway survive.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Favor AI-exposed businesses with funded runway; expect a shakeout among cash-burning startups.
insights.quote: There will come a time there'll be some form of a blowup a pretty highprofile one where people lose a whole bunch of money and that will cause a reset.

insights.claim: Advice to founders: raise capital now, but treat every dollar as your own and do not assume abundant capital will exist forever.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Signals Ackman sees the current funding window as cyclical, not permanent.

insights.claim: AI improvement pace is 'by far the fastest of anything I've ever seen', with updates of consequence in days rather than years (like overnight Tesla software updates).
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Rapid cadence shortens the window in which incumbents can adapt or investors can underwrite 10-year cash flows.
insights.quote: The pace of improvement is by far the fastest of anything I've ever seen.

insights.claim: Pershing Square used the 'SaaS apocalypse' repricing of software as an opportunity to buy Microsoft at what it viewed as an attractive valuation.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Shows a quality-at-a-price approach: use sector panics to buy dominant names, while still worrying about AI disruption.

insights.claim: Ackman expects large financial institutions' costs to fall meaningfully because AI (he cites Cognition rewriting COBOL into modern code in days rather than months) will cut legacy-system spending, but whether banks keep the savings depends on pricing power because money is a commodity.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains may be competed away to customers in commodity-like businesses; margin capture depends on pricing power.

insights.claim: Brookfield is an AI winner in Ackman's view because of infrastructure, power and financing capability, with 'effectively infinite demand for compute'.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Power and data-center infrastructure providers are a way to play AI without model risk.

themes.theme: Pershing Square investment process and philosophy

insights.claim: Pershing Square targets 'super durable growth companies': dominant, highly profitable, strong balance sheets, simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative, with a stated ambition of 20%+ returns and a discipline of owning only what it would hold if markets closed for 10 years.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Defines the screen behind a concentrated large-cap portfolio.

insights.claim: Process: keep a 'library' of high-quality companies followed for years, wait for a price dislocation (a macro event like Covid or the SaaS selloff) to reach a 20%+ return, then two analysts do a deep dive (filings, expert networks, competitors, former employees), present a deck, and the team debates.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Explains why large positions appear after sector drawdowns.

insights.claim: Pershing Square uses AI as a research tool but not to build models, arguing that when everyone has the same AI it is hard to differentiate and its best trades (CDS before the pandemic, bankrupt-company stock, shorting AAA credit before the financial crisis) were non-obvious ideas a model would not suggest.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Edge comes from variant perception, not from AI-derived consensus.
insights.quote: In a world where everyone has the same access to AI, it's hard to be differentiated.

insights.claim: Pershing Square's investment principles are engraved on a stone tablet after a large loss circa 2015-2016: simple predictable free-cash-flow companies, large-cap liquid public stocks, aversion to short selling, and asymmetric bets where the view differs from consensus.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Shows codified discipline and constraints on the fund's behavior.

insights.claim: Ackman avoids short selling because of reverse asymmetry (unlimited loss, capped gain); his fraudulent-pyramid-scheme short ended with a squeeze by Carl Icahn buying the stock, and most crisis-era profits came from credit default swaps rather than shorting stock.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates that even correct shorts can lose to market dynamics and crowded opponents.
insights.quote: We underestimated the risk of market dynamics, i.e. Carl icon showing up, buying the stock, putting capital to work uh against us.

insights.claim: Netflix case study: Pershing bought after a subscriber miss, exited weeks later when management reversed its 'never' stance on advertising (thesis broken), redeployed into Alphabet, then bought Netflix back after it executed well and the stock halved again.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Shows willingness to sell on broken thesis and re-buy at a price for a high-certainty business; Netflix and Alphabet are core holdings.

insights.claim: Ackman's advice for ordinary savers: index funds are a very good approach and have beaten most active investors; start young, do not hold cash because the market looks expensive, and only pick stocks if you will invest real time.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Consistent with a passive default for non-professionals.

themes.theme: Howard Hughes as a Berkshire-style insurance compounder

insights.claim: Howard Hughes was created in the General Growth restructuring by spinning out land, master-planned communities (MPCs) and non-core assets; Pershing Square now owns about 47% and is transforming it into a 'modern day Berkshire Hathaway'.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: A control-stake holding-company transformation whose value depends on insurance execution, not real estate multiples.
insights.quote: we're transforming into what we call a modern day Bergkshire Hathaway

insights.claim: Howard Hughes' MPC real estate business self-liquidates over time, generating roughly $300 million of net operating income and hundreds of millions in annual land and condo sales ($4 billion of Hawaii condos under contract); that cash will be redeployed into insurance rather than more real estate.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Cash-flow visibility funds the insurer's capital needs without issuing stock.

insights.claim: Howard Hughes bought specialty P&C insurer Vantage Holdings, added $300 million of capital, recruited what Ackman calls the best insurance management team, and expects a shift from about 70% real estate/30% insurance to roughly 70-75% insurance within about five years.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Signals a re-rating path from a disliked real estate stock toward an insurance-holding multiple.

insights.claim: Ackman's model of Berkshire's success: permanent capital, insurance float invested in treasuries plus common stocks, no dividends, no dilution, control that allows a long-term view, and talented operators; he thinks it is rarely copied because insurance investing is 'not sexy'.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanics Howard Hughes intends to replicate: negative-cost float plus good asset management can compound near 20%.

insights.claim: Charlie Munger told Ackman the most underrated aspect of Berkshire's success was that 'we were almost never forced to make decisions by circumstances'.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Permanent capital creates optionality in panics.
insights.quote: we were almost never forced to make decisions by circumstances so we always had options

themes.theme: Pershing Square structure, permanent capital and team

insights.claim: Pershing Square deliberately moved to permanent-capital public vehicles (Pershing Square Inc., two listed funds, Howard Hughes, Pershing Square USA with $500M+ employee investment) so capital cannot leave in panics, and Ackman attributes his biggest investment mistake to being distracted by fundraising.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Permanent capital lets the firm buy in crashes and grow fee streams via compounding rather than fundraising.

insights.claim: Ackman owns about 45% of the Pershing Square management company, the team owns about 35%, and no one is paid on individual stocks; he says compounding at historic rates could put the firm at $1 trillion under management in 20 years.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: High insider ownership and fee-stream growth tied to asset compounding.

insights.claim: The investment team has had no turnover for nine years, which Ackman says builds candid trust and lets him generate only a minority of ideas now.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Team stability is a key-person risk mitigant for the firm.

insights.claim: Ackman criticises typical closed-end fund boards (citing the same six directors sitting on 86 BlackRock fund boards) and says Pershing's listed funds have independent, properly paid directors.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Governance gaps in closed-end funds are the basis of activist discount plays.

insights.claim: Activism has shifted from public proxy fights to private dialogue: Ackman says no activist investment since 2016, CEOs now write thanking Pershing for investing, and he believes a proxy contest against someone with millions of Twitter followers 'ends badly for management'.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Signals Pershing's influence works by reputation and stake, so new positions may come with quieter influence.

insights.claim: Ackman argues short-term activism (cost-cutting, leverage, buybacks) that harms long-term value is pointless because index holders like Vanguard and BlackRock are 'forever owners' who will not support it.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Passive owners' long horizon constrains short-term activism.

insights.claim: Public-market investing at Pershing is about durable dominant companies where a bad CEO can be replaced, whereas venture is a bet on the founder and their ability to pivot; Ackman weights the person more than the idea, citing his best venture investment (Coupang) which began as a Groupon clone for South Korea.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates that early-stage returns come from founder adaptability, not the initial business model.

insights.claim: Pershing Square is starting to invest in venture-stage businesses in the current AI cycle.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: A signal that large public-market investors are extending into private AI exposure.

themes.theme: Brain institute, healthcare gaps and personal context

insights.claim: Ackman and Neri Oxman are building the Oxman brain rehabilitation, recovery and longevity institute in New York on a 3.4-acre site bought within about 60 days, after his daughter Lucy's brain hemorrhage from an arteriovenous malformation.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: A large personal capital commitment into brain computer interfaces, AI-assisted rehab and neuro care.

insights.claim: Neurosurgeons are paid for surgery, not long-term recovery, and insurers often cover only about six weeks of rehab, so typical patients end up in nursing homes; Ackman says AI speech therapy and technology can make rehabilitation broadly affordable.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Structural misaligned incentives in neuro rehab create an opening for tech-enabled care models.

insights.claim: Ackman says Elon Musk told him vision via brain-computer interface could give people 'bionic vision' within about five years, and notes a dozen companies beyond Neuralink working on brain-computer interfaces.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Secondhand timeline; watch neurotech as an adjacent AI application.

insights.claim: He notes an Oura ring pulse spike and drop could be combined with fall detection (as on Apple Watch) to flag a medical emergency, and that Oura is working on the capability.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Wearables' emergency-detection features are a product direction with consumer pull.

insights.claim: Ackman describes Brémont, a small watch company he bought effective control of after a board fight, as a 'hobby investment' with an improved product under a new CEO.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates activist habits applied to a small private holding; not material to Pershing's portfolio.

insights.claim: Ackman's recruiting approach for turnarounds is to hire someone who has done it before, using expert-network 360 references and an hour-long assessment of passion, energy, honesty and character (Brian Niccol at Chipotle as example).
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Explains Pershing's CEO-replacement playbook in portfolio companies.

insights.claim: Sports teams are valued more like artwork than financial enterprises, and Ackman says he will not buy one.
insights.speaker: guest, Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder
insights.so_what: Team valuations reflect non-financial returns, weakening cash-flow comps.
